📝我的行程
第1️⃣天：落地海拉尔机场，落地时间早领队安排去阿尔山，落地时间晚就在海拉尔休息第二天出发！
·
第2️⃣天：一整天深度玩转阿尔山秋景，早起看不动河的晨雾，河流边还有牛牛和漫山遍野的金黄橙红交织，午后光线柔和林间光影刚好，随手拍出森系治愈大片
·
第3️⃣天：阿尔山前往呼伦湖再到满洲里住宿，沿途是满目鎏金秋色，中午抵达呼伦湖，秋日湖面澄澈静谧小羊门悠闲踱步，傍晚抵达满洲里，逛异域风情街头，吃地道的内蒙火锅
·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·
第6️⃣天：上午欣赏额尔古纳草原初秋的湿地黄绿渐变河道蜿蜒，成群的牛马过水美的不像话，下午奔赴莫日格勒河俯瞰天下第一曲水壮阔又温柔，在落日余晖下我们疯狂拍照记录下开心时刻，返回海拉尔吃了心心念念的俄餐
第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程
·
Day1：海拉尔→阿尔山
Day2：阿尔山不动河→阿尔山国家森林公园
Day3：阿尔山→呼伦湖→满洲里
Day4：满洲里→呼伦湖→186彩带河➠黑山头
Day5：黑山头→恩和民族乡→白桦林→额尔古纳
Day6：额尔古纳→湿地→莫日格勒河→海拉尔
Day7：海拉尔→返程
·
秋季的内蒙早晚有温差，出游的伙伴记得带厚外套
·

items.title: I hate having to prove my brand loyalty just for the chance to buy hardware at full price
items.author: Jess Kinghorn
items.summary: Nobody likes scalpers, man—it's already hard enough to get the latest and greatest hardware, let alone with some enterprising bad actor and their bots buying
items.text:
Nobody likes scalpers, man—it's already hard enough to get the latest and greatest hardware, let alone with some enterprising bad actor and their bots buying up all the available stock, and then charging an even greater fortune for sought-after bits of kit. That said, I'm not really a big fan of the anti-scalper measures many vendors are now deploying either.

For instance, Sony Japan has rolled out an anti-scalper lottery system for PS5 Pro orders. To be in with even a chance of picking up the pricey console, you'll need a Sony account registered in Japan that has logged at least 60 hours or more of gaming, either on a PS4, a PS5, or both (via Tom's Hardware). In theory, that should be enough of a faff to deter scalpers and an easy enough hurdle for PlayStation fans to overcome. In practice, I'm not loving the weird precedent of locking my potential hardware purchases behind a dystopian brand loyalty test.

Obviously, it's not just Sony that's up to such silliness. Most recently, Valve implemented a reservation system for the launch of the Steam Frame. To sign up, the FAQ says, "You must have a Steam account in good standing," and that "You must have made a purchase on Steam prior to April 27th 2026."

To be fair to Valve, I did see reports of the Steam Machine being scalped for over $3,000. But 'In good standing'? What does that even mean? I couldn't find a precise definition from Valve itself; an account 'in good standing' could mean one not subject to a ban or any community restrictions, or it could mean an account that has made a purchase within a recent timeframe, or it could mean whatever suits Valve at any given moment. I'm still a little unclear on this finer point.

I've already written about how it's been genuinely cheaper for me to fly internationally to either QuakeCon or PAX West earlier this year, and pick up an RTX 5090 for MSRP at either of those in-person events. The latter scheme was described as 'Verified Priority Access IRL'. For those who don't recall, VPA was the draw system Nvidia used to offer the chance to pay full price for RTX 5090 or RTX 5080 Founders Edition graphics cards last year (Newegg's Shuffle lottery system also did a similar thing).

「PlayStation®5 Pro」のソニーストアでの購入申し込みを、本日9月28日（月）より受け付けます。ご応募・ご購入には条件がございます。ご応募数が販売予定台数を超えた場合は抽選となりますので、あらかじめご了承ください。詳しくはこちら⇒ https://t.co/h4rOIltI9Q https://t.co/71VaLlu5edSeptember 28, 2026

Zotac even attempted to beat those dastardly GPU scalpers by selling RTX 50-series graphics cards to actual gamers via Discord last year. And like Nvidia, Zotac likely knew it could sell every card it offered up through such a direct (not to mention exclusive) channel.

I hate this trend, even if it is all meant to deter scalpers. I firmly believe gaming, and PC gaming especially, should be for everyone, though I'll acknowledge it rarely lives up to that ideal. Brand loyalty tests like this, plus the runaway pricing caused by the ongoing memory supply crisis, mean those without deep reserves of both cash and time are still stuck on the outside looking in. Bottom line, though scalpers may be mostly closed out of the loop by reservation systems with set qualifying criteria, I'm not convinced this is the best deal for hardware consumers.

items.title: Popular Pokémon Game Officially Being Taken Offline Forever On October 3
items.author: Ewan Moore

items.text:
Published Oct 2, 2026, 4:34 AM EDT

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section. He still quite hasn’t gotten out of his mid 00’s emo phase, and knows more about The Legend of Zelda and Doctor Who than is probably healthy.
Ewan oversees the content operation of ScreenRant's gaming output, working with a talented team of writers and editors to cover everything from the latest GTA 6 news to the indie games you need on your radar.
Former Editor of GAMINGbible, Ewan also has words at Kotaku, Den of Geek, NME, and UNILAD. He's appeared on various podcasts, including VGC's and BBC's Let's Talk About Tech.

I don't know if you've noticed this, but there are an awful lot of Pokémon games out there. If we include spin-offs, there have been well over 100 Pokémon games released in the last 30 years. We've had pinball, racing, cozy life sims, dungeon crawlers, arena brawlers, real-time strategy, and whatever the hell Hey You, Pikachu! was supposed to be. Still not sure about that one.

Now, a more recent Pokémon game has officially confirmed it will be shutting down for good on October 3. And while this one might not be entirely approved of by The Pokémon Company (by which I mean it's an unofficial fan project) it's still a hugely popular game, and its loss will come as a blow to the Pokémon community.

Pokémon Wordle is a Japanese puzzle game that was released back in January 2022, and is one of the many, many variants on the successful Wordle formula. In Pokémon Wordle, you have to guess a Pokémon's name within a set number of turns. To be clear, this is not the same as Pokedle, which is an entirely different free-to-play fan game that is loosely based on Wordle without being a direct clone.

Twitter user giga_yadoran, who created Pokémon Wordle, confirmed that the game will be shutting down as of tomorrow (October 3). While one might assume this request came via the typically litigious Pokémon Company, it was actually Wordle rights holder The New York Times who got in touch to ask the game be removed.

"We received contact from the New York Times regarding Wordle rights, so Pokémon Wordle will end its public release on 10/3 (Sat)," giga wrote. "Thank you to everyone who played it until now!"

"Over the years, you've entertained me greatly," replied one fan. "Thank you so very, very much."

Another fan took aim at The New York Times, writing: "Wordle itself is just an analog game turned into a digital one, and all that happened was the New York Times acquired it. It doesn't have any novelty, nor does it have any patents, and in the first place, given that Wordle itself is a rip-off game, I think the New York Times claiming copyright infringement against games similar to Wordle is way too thuggish..."

Certainly, there are loads of versions of Wordle still out there. My personal favorite is Poople, in which you have to make the word poop in the shortest possible path from a starting word while only changing one letter at a time.

As far as official Pokémon game releases, the next big one is Winds & Waves for the Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027. Sadly, despite many leaks since the game's one and only official trailer, it's unlikely we see more of the upcoming Gen 10 game until early next year. If only we had some kind of Wordle clone to help pass the time.

items.title: Lord Of The Rings Officially Replaces The Fellowship In New War Of The Ring-Era Release
items.author: Jared Stewart
items.summary: The era of middling Lord of the Rings games, much less barely any Lord of the Rings games at all, may finally be over. The Lord of the Rings: Return to Moria
items.text:
The era of middling Lord of the Rings games, much less barely any Lord of the Rings games at all, may finally be over. The Lord of the Rings: Return to Moria and Tales of the Shire: A The Lord of the Rings Game were spectacular in their own way, to be fair, particularly in terms of there actually being interesting gameplay genres explored by the IP, but it wasn’t until Aspyr’s Lord of the Rings: War in the North re-release launched that it became clear how bright The Lord of the Rings’ future is now in the realm of video games.

Warhorse’s open-world Middle-earth RPG is a stunningly bright light on the horizon, for instance, yet there’s now quite a real possibility that we’ll have Aspyr-led re-releases and/or remasters of classic Lord of the Rings games for years to come. In the meantime, to commemorate The Lord of the Rings: War in the North - Legacy Edition’s unanticipated revival, fans also have a special Deluxe edition to look forward to.

Per its website, physical distributor Limited Run Games has unveiled that preorders are officially live for a Deluxe edition of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North - Legacy Edition. Priced at $112.99 USD, the Deluxe edition includes:

Standard edition of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North - Legacy Edition with a slipcase and a Wayfinder’s Ledger booklet

Steelcase

Cloth map

Weathered letter with a foreword penned by Jed Brophy

Anyone hoping to nab themselves a Deluxe edition of The Lord of the Rings: War in the North - Legacy Edition shouldn’t wait too long, though. Pre-orders for it have a limited window, between today and December 13 (at 11:59 PM EST, specifically), meaning you only have a couple of months to secure yours.

Aspyr Media

No release date is available, with the website merely stating that it is “coming soon.” Not only is it fantastic that Limited Run Games champions physical releases and preservation, but it’s also maybe a hopeful sign that any subsequent Lord of the Rings re-releases from Aspyr will receive their own Deluxe edition soon thereafter.

As long as there is interest and demand for such physical goodies, at least, and pre-orders may determine whether or not other classic Lord of the Rings games get the same treatment. It’d be massively disappointing if fans were finally graced with a re-release of The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King and it didn’t have something like this, but it’s no less incredible for The Lord of the Rings: War in the North.

items.title: There are so many games coming out in October you guys
items.author: Andrea Shearon
items.summary: We've only got three months left in the year, but our list of upcoming 2026 games has enough October releases and updates to tide me over until this time next
items.text:
We've only got three months left in the year, but our list of upcoming 2026 games has enough October releases and updates to tide me over until this time next year. I just installed Silent Hill: Townfall, but who knows if I'll get to it before we start decking the halls or whatever the song says. I was hoping to deck a few monsters in Scotland. Alas.

It's a very my-steak-is-too-juicy complaint, but I've already overcommitted my October schedule to more survival crafting with Enshrouded's 1.0 update. I'm also trying to make time for MMO nostalgia when MapleStory Classic is out, and Final Fantasy Resonance will have to squeeze in there somewhere.

My own calendar is already buckling under the weight of this month's treats, so in the spirit of spooky season, I haunted a few colleagues with threats of dead pixels and ghosting until they shared their staff picks for the month. I'm pacified, for now. But I'll be back again next month with a turkey and the world's most mumbly protagonist.

October 2026 PC Gamer picks

October 6

Star Wars: Galactic Racer

Steam | I'm not a big Star Wars fan, but I have a soft spot for 1999's Star Wars: Episode I Racer and other sci-fi racing games of the era, like F-Zero. I'm hoping for cool crashes—like 50% of the fun of these things is exploding spectacularly—and I'm curious to know what the 'run based' structure entails. — Tyler Wilde

October 9

Car Park Capital

Steam | There's nothing more American than cars and this satirical city builder, like so many US cities, centers around them. Turn a walkable town into an automotive paradise by using car-positive propaganda to convince citizens their homes should be bulldozed in favor of towering parking garages. — Christopher Livingston

October 13

Valor Mortis

Steam | My appetite for Soulslike games is not enormous these days, but first-person takes are more intriguing to me, especially when they pick a setting as original as the Napoleonic wars (except supernatural). The creators of the Ghostrunner games have picked a new and exciting lane with Valor Mortis – I just hope it's not too difficult. — Samuel Roberts

items.title: Advocacy Group Stop Killing Games Sounds Alarm On EU Kids Act: ‘This Is Such A Horrible Law Proposal’
items.author: Lewis Parker
items.summary: In a recently released video, the consumer advocacy group Stop Killing Games and its creator, YouTuber Ross Scott, have expressed concern with the European
items.text:
In a recently released video, the consumer advocacy group Stop Killing Games and its creator, YouTuber Ross Scott, have expressed concern with the European Union’s recently proposed EU Kids Act, which Scott has referred to as a “bomb that could implode the whole video games industry.”

The EU Kids Act was officially proposed on September 17, 2026. According to the outline provided for the EU Kids Act on the official European Commission website, the proposal in question primarily “seeks to protect minors from risky digital services and AI systems, uphold the digital single market and maintain a coherent regulatory framework and enforcement structure for the protection of minors online.”

However, Stop Killing Games’ Ross Scott stated in a new video that the EU Kids Act is using the ever-looming threat of AI and the protection of “minors from risky digital services” as a “cover” for its true aims, referring to these things as a “mask to hide what else is in there.”

“Curbing social media and AI has nothing to do with why this is such a horrible law proposal,” stated Scott. “As it stands, the EU Kids Act is the most draconian proposal I’ve ever seen regarding video games and consumers.” Among Scott’s chief concerns is that the proposal will “require your personal identifying information to play an online video game” and “make all private game servers illegal.”

While Scott’s comments were initially based on a leaked version of the EU Kids Act proposal, the segments from it featured in his video do line up exactly with the official version of the proposal that has since been published on the European Commission website. Said proposal is indeed quite broad in its application, as it states that it “sets out clear safety by design requirements for online social networking services, video-sharing platform services, online games, AI companions and general conversational chatbots, and software application stores.”

It’s important to bear in mind that the proposal is a 99-page document, and there’s a lot of legalese to contend with. That being said, the main section in question where video games are concerned is Chapter III, titled “Safety By Design.” But, as Scott explains, there’s a confusing wrinkle in this proposal that has to be tackled before we even get to that: how does the EU Kids Act define a “video game”?

According to the “definitions” section of the proposal, a “video game” is “an information society service.” The use of the term “information society service” here is quite specific, as the EU GDPR defines it as “any service normally provided for remuneration, at a distance, by electronic means and at the individual request of a recipient of services.” In simpler terms, an “information society service” is something that can be purchased online.

So, does this apply to digitally purchased games that have no online features? Scott argues that said definition “is as clear as mud,” which is why Stop Killing Games is concerned that the EU Kids Act’s age verification requirements can be broadly applied to any game purchased through a digital storefront. Obviously, this is an extremely pertinent concern considering that Steam is a purely digital storefront, and Sony is ending disc production for all new PlayStation games in 2028.

Of course, the EU Kids Act is in no way final. It is, quite literally, a proposal, which means it’s still in the earliest stage of the European Union’s legislative process. Before it even reaches both the European Parliament’s and the EU Council’s voting stages, it will be reviewed and, most likely, amended.

And, as Scott stated in his conclusion, that’s exactly why Stop Killing Games believes that tackling the EU Kids Act now is a priority: “The best thing you can do is spread the word on this. The people who write this crap do not like it when the public at large knows what they’re trying to do to you. If everyone in gaming understood what the EU Kids Act is trying to do, it wouldn’t have a chance of passing. So, let’s let people know!”

items.title: RetroSpace offers a huge sci-fi playground for inquisitive space janitors, but I'm not that System Shocked by the tools at your disposal
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot
items.text:
In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot dinners. As such, any videogame that can get me excited about loosening a barred hatch and hauling my heavy ass into a square tunnel is doing something right.

The Wild Gentlemen's new sci-fi immersive sim RetroSpace gives pretty fair vent. It hides them all over. You'll walk along a dilapidated, meandering corridor and your eye will be caught by a certain combination of shadows, flirtatiously screened by pipes. 'Can I fit behind there?' You ask yourself, and lo, you have revealed a shortcut to the head engineer's office. Elsewhere, switches peek from behind stacks of luggable crates, and bent guard-rails draw your eye to a footwide ledge leading around the next pillar.

In general, RetroSpace does a nice job of squirrelling secrets into even the smallest chambers, and if the secret is very often a "rocket doughnut" or other inventory-clogging flotsam, sensing the prize and snuffling after it is a thrill. I hope the thrill will intensify as RetroSpace goes on, perhaps leaving a few of its obvious influences behind.

Watch on YouTube

RetroSpace takes place aboard Aurora 5, a pseudo-1970s interstellar ark that has tumbled into a black hole, and somehow come away with a mild case of temporal indecision – certain areas flip between timeframes - rather than spaghettification and incomprehensible doom. You are a janitor, woken from cryo to find a lot of stuff on fire, a lot of people dead, and a lot of other people deranged and monsterfied by gene-modding. Taking up your power wrench, you set out for the habitat hub and soon become embroiled in missions assigned by a handful of coherent survivors, including a sentient AI and a talking pig fellah.

These take you out to the far corners of the space station, which is very much the main character here. There's a "garden" sector that consists of a verdant silo with a starry dome, its spiral stairs and crawlspaces leading down to what I think is a bubbling soup of fertiliser. There's a train that circles the whole facility – not a camouflaged loading screen, as with chapter breaks in Dead Space, but an actual monorail car that travels in real time. There are a lot of audiologs, hackable terminals, and comedy public safety signs or adverts. As you might expect from the devisers of chicken detective games, RetroSpace skews toward caricature, which can get obnoxious – there's an audiolog early on that pokes fun at NPCs who leave scary audiologs. Still, it feels like the devs are fundamentally committed to making an engrossing world.

There's a persistent mystique woven around the station's janitors. Propaganda posters cast you and your lost brethren as urban legends, seldom seen by regular folk because you're always up a ladder or behind a bulkhead doing whatever it is you helmeted weirdos do with those sprays and spanners. Each sector has a locked or concealed utility closet with a portal to the Janitor's Haven - an interdimensional hideaway set up by union organisers, where you'll hang out with story-critical NPCs and do the bulk of your upgrading and customising.

If the station is a peach, I'm a little less convinced so far by the tools at your disposal. On the one hand, you've got weapons such as pistols, shotguns, and rayguns, all (eventually) upgradeable. On the other, you've got more indirect or tactical accessories such as cloaking devices, computer-hacking gizmos, and propulsive fire extinguishers. On the third hand, you've got genetic engineering or Mutamods, which range from giving yourself grasshopper thighs for higher jumping, moth ears so that you heal in light, or biceps full of rhino DNA for meatier clobbering.

The gene-modding cuts both ways: when you die, you'll be cloned for free at the nearest Bacta tank equivalent, but you'll be saddled with a random cartoon affliction for your troubles. I came away from one misadventure with a body prone to uncontrollable sneezing and swearing, which did not help with subsequent attempts at stealth. Fortunately, you can purge the debuffs by siphoning genetic material from the nearest vanilla human corpse, and Aurora 5 has no shortage of those.

Within the world, you can also do things like hold up crates to block bullets, or spray paths of water to create an electricity trap before smacking a circuit box. It's all entertaining enough, but many of the ideas are overly familiar from System Shock, Bioshock and Arkane's Prey. I'm really hoping that somewhere in RetroSpace, there lurks a tool or combination of tools that is as daft in its own way as Prey's Mimic ability. Or the slapstick bullshit you get in Skin Deep.

As it is, I'm finding that I'm too often just shooting enemies because I'm unexcited by the more devious ways of avoiding or defeating them. The enemies have their moments – lop a bugman's head off, and it might sprout legs, while the manpigs are drawn to trails of blood - but a lot of the time, they're just awareness indicators you can either avoid or gun down.

If you're comfortable with how comfortable RetroSpace can feel, as a love letter to certain famous immersive sims, you'll likely be able to forgive all this. Myself, I'd say the station ambience and secretive level design are worth the occasional sense of deja-vu. I'll keep plugging on with the game, though games journalism being what it currently is, I sadly don't have time for a full review. Find out more about RetroSpace on Steam. Let me know if you spot any really sexy airvents.

items.title: I perished in the flesh pipes of Darktide's Depths of the Damned update, and you will too
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide continues to cling tightly, perhaps even aggressively, to my Steam installations, my occasionally waning interest repeatedly
items.text:
Warhammer 40,000: Darktide continues to cling tightly, perhaps even aggressively, to my Steam installations, my occasionally waning interest repeatedly re-sparked by the addition of akimbo-autopistolling chem fiends or haughty toasterpeople. A live service sucker, it makes me. Today's Depths of the Damned update, the grimdark co-op shooter's biggest since the Skitarii rocked up, continues the trend: it's centered around a massive new mission that's as revolting as it is compelling.

Whereas most Darktide excursions take you through criss-crossing sectors of its impossibly gigantic Hive City, the new Spillway deployment dumps you in the gushing, thus-unexplored hell of Tertium's water treatment facility. It’s a spectacular place, in the sense that it's utterly horrible. Fetid green liquid rushes through its caverns as blasphemous new life sprouts from the moisture, dark moss covering the cages that the complex's former gangster ownership probably didn’t hang for aesthetic reasons. The current residents aren't much friendlier, taking full advantage of the space's long sightlines to pelt you with lasgun fire while their fellow crusty cultists charge into melee range.

The Spillway's guts are even nastier. I'd say they’re covered in daemonic growths, but that would suggest the existence of visible points where the Chaos meat first took root. It would be more accurate to say the growths have become structurally integral to the facility in general, entire rooms covered floor-to-ceiling in the muck. The pipe network, meanwhile, is so thickly coated that it starts resembling a badly diseased intestinal tract; a playable Fantastic Voyage, if Raquel Welch was an Ogryn.

Despite this, and with the caveat that I've only played through the new mission once, it doesn't have the radically different feel of certain other post-launch operation additions. 2024's Rolling Steel was a runaway train caper unlike anything Darktide had tried before, and the Hive Scum update's No Man's Land op successfully swapped metal corridors for muddy trenches in a breathless WW1-inspired rush. Spillway is, at least structurally, a much more conventional oscillation of fierce wave combat and quieter traversal.

Those other two missions, however, were comparatively tight, short-form jaunts. This is a full-length, maybe even bumper-sized new challenge, which does at least try to enact some smaller twists along the way. There's a spot of light memory-puzzling, for example, as you’re shown a particular daub of gang graffiti that will mark the safe-ish path through the mazelike pipes – if you can find it among all the other gang graffiti. I don’t know if it’s a guaranteed spawn, but I was also ambushed partway through the upper facility by a traitor Captain, a foe usually reserved as the final boss for Assassination and Rolling Steel runs.

Spillway's actual final boss, which I’m slightly loathe to spoil (outside of the odd screenshot, naturally), almost manages to be a burst of freshness in a warren of filth. He's probably the most bosslike among all of Darktide's chunkiest baddies, advancing through phases, throwing out ruinous AoE attacks, and cackling through invulnerable periods like the mad space wizard he is. May your squads be smarter and more attentive than my gang of AI bots, or you’ll end up like me: a psychically flayed corpse, fallen without glory inside a lair made of poo chutes.

It’s a tricky one, basically, even with my Welch-Orgyn equipping two of the update’s new weapons – both slightly overtuned, as is Darktide patch tradition. The Thugshot is a slug-firing, crowd-penetrating breachloader, capable of slicing through shamblers like it's hitting the 'Delete column' button in Excel, while the Cruncher sledgehammer can thwack lesser enemies clean off ledges in a satisfying sideswipe. Both pay for their heavy damage by imparting it slowly, but then that just encourages you to find the rhythm in Darktide’s swingin'.

Either way, I have unfinished business with Far Future Thames Water and their rotting, three-phase CEO. Attending to it, even with the greater time investment and/or firmer teeth-clenching requirements over previous new missions, seems like a good way to make the most of Darktide's continued SSD presence.

There's a spot of light memory-puzzling, for example, as you’re shown a particular daub of gang graffiti that will mark the safe-ish path through the mazelike pipes – if you can find it among all the other gang graffiti. I don’t know if it’s a guaranteed spawn, but I was also ambushed partway through the upper facility by a traitor Captain, a foe usually reserved as the final boss for Assassination and Rolling Steel runs.

Spillway's actual final boss, which I’m slightly loathe to spoil (outside of the odd screenshot, naturally), almost manages to be a burst of freshness in a warren of filth. He's probably the most bosslike among all of Darktide's chunkiest baddies, advancing through phases, throwing out ruinous AoE attacks, and cackling through invulnerable periods like the mad space wizard he is. May your squads be smarter and more attentive than my gang of AI bots, or you’ll end up like me: a psychically flayed corpse, fallen without glory inside a lair made of poo chutes.

It’s a tricky one, basically, even with my Welch-Orgyn equipping two of the update’s new weapons – both slightly overtuned, as is Darktide patch tradition. The Thugshot is a slug-firing, crowd-penetrating breachloader, capable of slicing through shamblers like it's hitting the 'Delete column' button in Excel, while the Cruncher sledgehammer can thwack lesser enemies clean off ledges in a satisfying sideswipe. Both pay for their heavy damage by imparting it slowly, but then that just encourages you to find the rhythm in Darktide’s swingin'.

Either way, I have unfinished business with Far Future Thames Water and their rotting, three-phase CEO. Attending to it, even with the greater time investment and/or firmer teeth-clenching requirements over previous new missions, seems like a good way to make the most of Darktide's continued SSD presence.

items.title: Adult Swim’s “Get Jiro” Serves Up Bloody, Sloppy Culinary Revenge
items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One,
items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

items.title: 8 Netflix Shows That Deserve a Place Among TV's All-Time Greatest, Ranked
items.author: Jiminna Shillingford
items.summary:
Published Oct 2, 2026, 6:09 AM EDT

Jiminna Shillingford is an avid reader and a passionate storyteller. She is obsessed with all things TV, from anime and
items.text:
Published Oct 2, 2026, 6:09 AM EDT

Jiminna Shillingford is an avid reader and a passionate storyteller. She is obsessed with all things TV, from anime and romantic fantasy to action-packed series. With that deep affection, Jiminna longs to share her excitement with all her readers through the Collider platform as a TV author. Through her writing she has created stories and blog posts of amazing book recommendations, showcasing her love of writing. Jiminna's goal is to inspire others to discover and embrace their love of stories in all of its forms.

Among some of Netflix's finest releases, there are a select few that truly stand out, solid gems that are often discussed alongside some of TV's all-time greatest. The streaming platform's select few go way beyond being simply popular or binge-worthy — they offer unforgettable characters, sharp writing, bold visuals, emotional depth, and a truly impressive level of storytelling that lingers with viewers long after the credits roll.

Netflix series like the video game adaptation Arcane, which stuns with its epically beautiful visuals, and the brilliant but terribly bleak animated icon BoJack Horseman, which is just as darkly humorous as it is devastating, are two gems on the platform that prove that streaming television can stand among some of the most respected shows ever created. Compiled on this list are some of Netflix's finest all-time greats that definitely deserve a place among TV's best. The shows are ranked based on the strength of their writing, performances, visual identity, cultural impact, consistency, and overall contribution to Netflix's reputation for prestige television.

8
'Blue Eye Samurai' (2023–Present)

Image via Netflix

Blue Eye Samurai is one of Netflix’s more recent animated masterpieces that already stands as one of the platform’s greats. Blue Eye Samurai is set in 17th-century Edo-period Japan, following the sword master, Mizu (Maya Erskine), who is traveling disguised as a man as she pursues foreign men who may be connected to her birth.

Blue Eye Samurai earns its place in this discussion of TV’s all-time greatest because it transforms revenge into something beautiful, emotionally captivating, and extraordinarily brutal. The series masterfully connects action to shame, identity, rejection, and survival. Blue Eye Samurai may essentially be the “new kid” on the block, but it's definitely left its mark on those who have happened across the incredibly entertaining action series. Its composition borrows from Japanese art, chanbara, westerns, graphic novels, and live-action blocking, all without ever settling into imitation, marking it as one of the most powerful viewing experiences that masterfully carries the weight of classic samurai storytelling.

7
'Sense8' (2015–2018)

Image via Netflix

Sense8 easily makes this list, even when it's one of Netflix’s most underrated sci-fi gems. The series follows eight strangers across the globe — police officer Will Gorski (Brian J. Smith), DJ Riley Blue (Tuppence Middleton), hacker Nomi Marks (Jamie Clayton), actor Lito Rodriguez (Miguel Ángel Silvestre), pharmacist Kala Dandekar (Tina Desai), businesswoman and fighter Sun Bak (Bae Doona), safe-cracker Wolfgang Bogdanow (Max Riemelt), and bus driver Capheus Onyango (Toby Onwumere) — as they realize they share a connection that allows them to experience one another’s memories, skills, emotions, thoughts, languages, and danger.

From epic visuals to a masterful action story, Sense8 stands as a quality series that is far too rarely talked about. The show lingers among the greatest of TV because it's genuinely one of Netflix’s most ambitious works of art. Very few television shows even come close to matching its boldness and sincerity. With its premise exploring love, culture, sexuality, and identity across different lives and countries, Sense8 earns its status as a rare great that is worthy of all-time recognition.

6
'Ozark' (2017–2022)

Image via Netflix

This crime drama leaves its mark on its viewers because it consistently builds tension. Ozark centers around Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman), a financial adviser, who moves his family to the Missouri Ozarks after a money-laundering scheme for the Mexican drug cartel goes wrong and forces him to launder millions more, while desperately trying to keep himself and his family safe.

Ozark is one of the best crime series produced by Netflix, and it has earned its spot in discussions regarding the platform’s all-time greatest because it transforms what could have been a pretty generic crime premise into a relentless story about survival, family, and moral collapse. The show is a bundle of tension as it makes every choice feel dangerous, even when characters are in mostly quiet moments, biding their time. Ozark is quite the thrilling watch that Netflix subscribers have frequently praised for its efforts in showcasing an intense and incredibly unpredictable crime story, easily making it a genuinely fantastic all-time great among TV’s best, for that alone.

5
'Stranger Things' (2016–2025)

Image via Netflix

This extremely iconic sci-fi series is so deserving of its spot among TV’s finest because it’s somehow so much more than one of Netflix’s biggest hits — it became one of the shows most tied to the platform itself. Stranger Things follows the disappearance of Will Byers (Noah Schnapp), which leads his friends, local cops, mother, and brother to a mysterious girl with supernatural abilities called Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown).

Stranger Things is a sci-fi experience unlike any other. It’s a brilliant mixture of coming-of-age drama, sci-fi, horror, and 1980s nostalgia. The show has impressive cultural reach for a series that initially started out as a small-town mystery, only to explode into a massive sci-fi horror adventure that viewers find difficult to turn away from. Stranger Things definitely belongs on this list of Netflix's greatest because it helped define what a modern streaming icon could look like on TV.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Netflix Character Would Be Your Best Friend?
Dustin · Emily · Wednesday · Gi-hun

Some friends drag you out of the house. Some sit with you on the worst night of your life. Netflix has written both, plus the one who tells you the truth you have been avoiding all week. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually do friendship, and find out which of them was always going to end up in your corner.

🧢Dustin(Stranger Things)

🗼Emily(Emily in Paris)

🕷️Wednesday(Wednesday)

🟢Gi-hun(Squid Game)

FIND YOUR BEST FRIEND →

01

How do you usually end up making a new friend?
The origin story says a lot about the friendship that follows it.

AWe got loud about the same obsession and never stopped.
BThey invited me somewhere before we had properly met.
CWe bonded over disliking exactly the same thing.
DThey noticed I was struggling and stayed with me.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What is a perfect Saturday with your best friend?
Friendship is mostly built out of very ordinary hours.

AA ridiculous plan neither of us should attempt.
BSomewhere new, photographed heavily, ending very late.
CSomewhere quiet, few people, zero small talk.
DSomething simple, and a conversation that actually matters.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

You call them at two in the morning. What happens?
This is the real test of a friendship, and everybody knows it.

AThey are already putting their shoes on.
BThey answer instantly and turn it into a plan.
CThey answer and say something unflattering and true.
DThey listen for an hour and never check the time.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

What do you want from them when you are clearly wrong?
The best friendships are the ones that survive being corrected.

ASupport first. We can review the mistake later.
BA relentlessly positive reframe of the entire disaster.
CThe blunt version. Do not soften it for me.
DPatience, and no judgment about how I got here.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

What do your friends actually value about you?
The friend you attract says something about the friend you are.

AI am all in, always, about everything.
BI can turn almost any situation into a good time.
CI say the thing nobody else in the room will.
DI look after whoever is having the worst day.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

You have a falling out. How does it go?
How a friendship repairs itself matters more than how it breaks.

ALoudly, briefly, then back to normal by Tuesday.
BThey apologise first, enthusiastically, with a gift.
CCold silence, then one dry joke that fixes everything.
DWe talk until we both understand what actually happened.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What do you actually need a best friend for?
Everybody is missing something. The right friend fills that gap.

ATo make my life bigger than it would be alone.
BTo push me out of the house and into my own life.
CTo catch me when I start lying to myself.
DTo be the person who never gave up on me.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Ten years from now, what keeps the two of you close?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides who you get.

AWe would still drop everything for each other, instantly.
BWe still make plans, and we still actually go.
CWe still cut through each other's nonsense in one sentence.
DThey stood by me once when it cost them something.

REVEAL MY BEST FRIEND →

The Group Chat Has Spoken
Your Best Friend Is…

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up
for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your
life would be like.

Stranger Things · Netflix · Since 2016

Dustin Henderson

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he.
What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the
plan.

Dustin is the friend the entire show runs on: loyal past the point of sense,
enthusiastic about everything, and incapable of leaving anybody behind.

You have the same instinct. Your friendships are loud, specific and slightly ridiculous,
and they last for decades because of it.

He is also the one person who would take your strangest interest completely seriously,
which is far rarer than it sounds.

You would have a group chat. It would never once be quiet.

Emily in Paris · Netflix · Since 2020

Emily Cooper

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she.
Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with
yourselves.

Emily treats an ordinary Tuesday as something that could be turned into an occasion,
which is either the best or the worst quality in a friend depending on your energy
levels.

You share her refusal to sit still. Neither of you has ever accepted a night in when
something was happening somewhere else.

She is far more loyal than people give her credit for. She defends her friends loudly,
publicly, and occasionally before checking the facts.

She would post the photo without asking. You would forgive her, because it is a very
good photo.

Wednesday · Netflix · Since 2022

Wednesday Addams

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to
tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this
list.

Wednesday never says a kind thing she does not mean, which makes the rare ones count for
an enormous amount.

You would rather be told the truth than be made comfortable. She is constitutionally
incapable of offering you anything else.

Underneath all of it she is ferociously protective. She simply refuses to make a
performance out of caring.

Do not expect a birthday message. Do expect her to ruin anyone who wrongs you.

Squid Game · Netflix · 2021–2025

Seong Gi-hun

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is
the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Gi-hun is not the strongest player in Squid Game, or the cleverest. He is the one who
keeps choosing to protect somebody else, over and over, at genuine cost to himself.

You have the same instinct. You notice who is struggling and you stay with them, long
after anybody would blame you for leaving.

He is a flawed friend, and that is part of why it lands. He lets people down, then comes
back and tries again, which is more than most manage.

He would give you his last chance and never once mention that he had done it.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

4
'Black Mirror' (2011–Present)

Image via Netflix

Black Mirror is Netflix's brilliant anthology sci-fi series that’s quite easy to debate, discuss, and genuinely remember. Each of the series' episodes is a complete story, which often uses technology, artificial intelligence, media, surveillance, and digital obsession to expose something quite chilling about human behavior.

Black Mirror is practically a Netflix icon, one that often delivers episodes that feel like short films which stay in the mind long after the credits roll. The anthology series may not have invented technological dystopia, but it definitely updated The Twilight Zone's model for social platforms, smartphones, virtual identity, machine learning, and platform capitalism with enough clarity that the series has become one of TV’s most unsettling and brilliantly recognizable examinations of humanity’s increasing dependence on modern tech. Black Mirror is absolutely one of Netflix’s bleakest series, but it also happens to be one of the platform's defining greats.

3
'Arcane' (2021–2024)

Image via Netflix

This Netflix animated series easily earns its place among TV’s all-time greatest. Adapted from the League of Legends universe, Arcane is set in the divided world of Piltover and Zaun, centering on sisters Vi (Hailee Steinfeld) and Powder, later known as Jinx (Ella Purnell), whose relationship is ripped apart due to tragedy as political tensions rise and conflict between the two cities threatens to change their lives forever.

Arcane is not only visually stunning, but it is also emotionally devastating. The Netflix animation is both confident and extremely controlled. There is no doubt that it's one of the streaming platform’s greatest masterpieces, which defiantly raised the bar for what animated TV and adaptations in general could achieve. Arcane is incredibly beautiful, so much so that viewers are able to pause at almost any frame and be hit with a face full of wonder. But in reality, its beauty isn’t even the show’s greatest strength; no, in fact, its most incredible achievements come from the tragedy of its characters and the consequences of their choices. Arcane is a memorable watch that lands itself on this list because, with visuals alone, it outpaces several in its genre.

2
'BoJack Horseman' (2014–2020)

Image via Netflix

BoJack Horseman masterfully mixes absurdity, sadness, emotional realism, and satire, becoming one of Netflix’s most defining animated shows. Set in a world populated by humans and anthropomorphic animals, the series focuses on BoJack Horseman (Will Arnett), a washed-up 1990s sitcom star, who is trying to reignite his fame while tackling addiction, loneliness, depression, and crippling depression.

BoJack Horseman does initially look like a pretty absurd Hollywood cartoon, but it's quite the emotional series. The show is actually extremely bleak, a mirror held up to its audience, as it doles out painfully honest examinations of depression, trauma, and the difficulty of trying to become a truly better person after repeatedly hurting those that matter. BoJack Horseman can easily claim its status as an all-time great because it’s incredibly raw and real, with a story that refuses to make light of rather serious topics and a protagonist who's extremely flawed, making it an icon in its own right.

1
'Mindhunter' (2017–2019)

Image via Netflix

This underrated masterpiece is definitely worthy of the status as one of the all-time greatest shows ever made because it transforms crime investigation into something deeply unsettling, quiet, and intelligent. Mindhunter focuses on FBI agents Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) and Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff), who begin interviewing imprisoned serial killers in the hopes of understanding how they think and using their findings to help solve ongoing murder cases.

Mindhunter doesn’t rely on constant scenes of fast-paced arrests or acts of violence, but instead spends its runtime focusing on the difficult conversations that eventually sparked change in how serial killers were being understood. The series stands out because very few Netflix dramas are as impeccably controlled or psychologically sharp, as it delivers a fantastic procedural idea but expertly elevates it with a chilling study of obsession, behavior, power, and the language people tend to use when explaining terrible deeds. Mindhunter is one of the most deserving to be recognized as an all-time great Netflix watch because there’s never a dull moment with the captivating series, with episode after episode of brilliant precision.

Release Date

2017 - 2019

Network

Netflix

Sense8 easily makes this list, even when it's one of Netflix’s most underrated sci-fi gems. The series follows eight strangers across the globe — police officer Will Gorski (Brian J. Smith), DJ Riley Blue (Tuppence Middleton), hacker Nomi Marks (Jamie Clayton), actor Lito Rodriguez (Miguel Ángel Silvestre), pharmacist Kala Dandekar (Tina Desai), businesswoman and fighter Sun Bak (Bae Doona), safe-cracker Wolfgang Bogdanow (Max Riemelt), and bus driver Capheus Onyango (Toby Onwumere) — as they realize they share a connection that allows them to experience one another’s memories, skills, emotions, thoughts, languages, and danger.

From epic visuals to a masterful action story, Sense8 stands as a quality series that is far too rarely talked about. The show lingers among the greatest of TV because it's genuinely one of Netflix’s most ambitious works of art. Very few television shows even come close to matching its boldness and sincerity. With its premise exploring love, culture, sexuality, and identity across different lives and countries, Sense8 earns its status as a rare great that is worthy of all-time recognition.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/ozark-jason-bateman-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jason Bateman looking to the side, about to get into a car in Ozark.

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

This crime drama leaves its mark on its viewers because it consistently builds tension. Ozark centers around Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman), a financial adviser, who moves his family to the Missouri Ozarks after a money-laundering scheme for the Mexican drug cartel goes wrong and forces him to launder millions more, while desperately trying to keep himself and his family safe.

Ozark is one of the best crime series produced by Netflix, and it has earned its spot in discussions regarding the platform’s all-time greatest because it transforms what could have been a pretty generic crime premise into a relentless story about survival, family, and moral collapse. The show is a bundle of tension as it makes every choice feel dangerous, even when characters are in mostly quiet moments, biding their time. Ozark is quite the thrilling watch that Netflix subscribers have frequently praised for its efforts in showcasing an intense and incredibly unpredictable crime story, easily making it a genuinely fantastic all-time great among TV’s best, for that alone.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F68acd0755fb2b-Jiminna%20Headshot.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

5
'Stranger Things' (2016–2025)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/stranger-things-season-5-millie-bobby-brown.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Millie Bobby Brown in Stranger Things Season 5

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

This extremely iconic sci-fi series is so deserving of its spot among TV’s finest because it’s somehow so much more than one of Netflix’s biggest hits — it became one of the shows most tied to the platform itself. Stranger Things follows the disappearance of Will Byers (Noah Schnapp), which leads his friends, local cops, mother, and brother to a mysterious girl with supernatural abilities called Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown).

Stranger Things is a sci-fi experience unlike any other. It’s a brilliant mixture of coming-of-age drama, sci-fi, horror, and 1980s nostalgia. The show has impressive cultural reach for a series that initially started out as a small-town mystery, only to explode into a massive sci-fi horror adventure that viewers find difficult to turn away from. Stranger Things definitely belongs on this list of Netflix's greatest because it helped define what a modern streaming icon could look like on TV.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Netflix Character Would Be Your Best Friend?
Dustin · Emily · Wednesday · Gi-hun

Some friends drag you out of the house. Some sit with you on the worst night of your life. Netflix has written both, plus the one who tells you the truth you have been avoiding all week. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually do friendship, and find out which of them was always going to end up in your corner.
🧢Dustin(Stranger Things)
🗼Emily(Emily in Paris)
🕷️Wednesday(Wednesday)
🟢Gi-hun(Squid Game)
FIND YOUR BEST FRIEND →

How do you usually end up making a new friend?
The origin story says a lot about the friendship that follows it.

AWe got loud about the same obsession and never stopped.
BThey invited me somewhere before we had properly met.
CWe bonded over disliking exactly the same thing.
DThey noticed I was struggling and stayed with me.
NEXT QUESTION →
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar49247643.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

What is a perfect Saturday with your best friend?
Friendship is mostly built out of very ordinary hours.

AA ridiculous plan neither of us should attempt.
BSomewhere new, photographed heavily, ending very late.
CSomewhere quiet, few people, zero small talk.
DSomething simple, and a conversation that actually matters.
NEXT QUESTION →

You call them at two in the morning. What happens?
This is the real test of a friendship, and everybody knows it.

AThey are already putting their shoes on.
BThey answer instantly and turn it into a plan.
CThey answer and say something unflattering and true.
DThey listen for an hour and never check the time.
NEXT QUESTION →

What do you want from them when you are clearly wrong?
The best friendships are the ones that survive being corrected.

ASupport first. We can review the mistake later.
BA relentlessly positive reframe of the entire disaster.
CThe blunt version. Do not soften it for me.
DPatience, and no judgment about how I got here.
NEXT QUESTION →

What do your friends actually value about you?
The friend you attract says something about the friend you are.

AI am all in, always, about everything.
BI can turn almost any situation into a good time.
CI say the thing nobody else in the room will.
DI look after whoever is having the worst day.
NEXT QUESTION →
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar51465563.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

You have a falling out. How does it go?
How a friendship repairs itself matters more than how it breaks.

ALoudly, briefly, then back to normal by Tuesday.
BThey apologise first, enthusiastically, with a gift.
CCold silence, then one dry joke that fixes everything.
DWe talk until we both understand what actually happened.
NEXT QUESTION →

What do you actually need a best friend for?
Everybody is missing something. The right friend fills that gap.

ATo make my life bigger than it would be alone.
BTo push me out of the house and into my own life.
CTo catch me when I start lying to myself.
DTo be the person who never gave up on me.
NEXT QUESTION →

Ten years from now, what keeps the two of you close?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides who you get.

AWe would still drop everything for each other, instantly.
BWe still make plans, and we still actually go.
CWe still cut through each other's nonsense in one sentence.
DThey stood by me once when it cost them something.
REVEAL MY BEST FRIEND →

The Group Chat Has Spoken
Your Best Friend Is…

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up
for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your
life would be like.
Stranger Things · Netflix · Since 2016
Dustin Henderson
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/netflix_logo-2.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he.
What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the
plan.

Dustin is the friend the entire show runs on: loyal past the point of sense,
enthusiastic about everything, and incapable of leaving anybody behind.

You have the same instinct. Your friendships are loud, specific and slightly ridiculous,
and they last for decades because of it.

He is also the one person who would take your strangest interest completely seriously,
which is far rarer than it sounds.
You would have a group chat. It would never once be quiet.
Emily in Paris · Netflix · Since 2020
Emily Cooper

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she.
Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with
yourselves.

Emily treats an ordinary Tuesday as something that could be turned into an occasion,
which is either the best or the worst quality in a friend depending on your energy
levels.

You share her refusal to sit still. Neither of you has ever accepted a night in when
something was happening somewhere else.

She is far more loyal than people give her credit for. She defends her friends loudly,
publicly, and occasionally before checking the facts.

She would post the photo without asking. You would forgive her, because it is a very
good photo.
Wednesday · Netflix · Since 2022
Wednesday Addams

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to
tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this
list.

Wednesday never says a kind thing she does not mean, which makes the rare ones count for
an enormous amount.

You would rather be told the truth than be made comfortable. She is constitutionally
incapable of offering you anything else.

Underneath all of it she is ferociously protective. She simply refuses to make a
performance out of caring.
Do not expect a birthday message. Do expect her to ruin anyone who wrongs you.
Squid Game · Netflix · 2021–2025
Seong Gi-hun

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is
the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Gi-hun is not the strongest player in Squid Game, or the cleverest. He is the one who
keeps choosing to protect somebody else, over and over, at genuine cost to himself.

You have the same instinct. You notice who is struggling and you stay with them, long
after anybody would blame you for leaving.

He is a flawed friend, and that is part of why it lands. He lets people down, then comes
back and tries again, which is more than most manage.
He would give you his last chance and never once mention that he had done it.

4
'Black Mirror' (2011–Present)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/img_8439-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: A man in a space suit in Black Mirror

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

Black Mirror is Netflix's brilliant anthology sci-fi series that’s quite easy to debate, discuss, and genuinely remember. Each of the series' episodes is a complete story, which often uses technology, artificial intelligence, media, surveillance, and digital obsession to expose something quite chilling about human behavior.

Black Mirror is practically a Netflix icon, one that often delivers episodes that feel like short films which stay in the mind long after the credits roll. The anthology series may not have invented technological dystopia, but it definitely updated The Twilight Zone's model for social platforms, smartphones, virtual identity, machine learning, and platform capitalism with enough clarity that the series has become one of TV’s most unsettling and brilliantly recognizable examinations of humanity’s increasing dependence on modern tech. Black Mirror is absolutely one of Netflix’s bleakest series, but it also happens to be one of the platform's defining greats.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/assets/images/sr-db-logo-icon-colored-dark.svg?v=1.9
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/jinx-sacrifice-arcane-finale-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Netflix

This Netflix animated series easily earns its place among TV’s all-time greatest. Adapted from the League of Legends universe, Arcane is set in the divided world of Piltover and Zaun, centering on sisters Vi (Hailee Steinfeld) and Powder, later known as Jinx (Ella Purnell), whose relationship is ripped apart due to tragedy as political tensions rise and conflict between the two cities threatens to change their lives forever.

Arcane is not only visually stunning, but it is also emotionally devastating. The Netflix animation is both confident and extremely controlled. There is no doubt that it's one of the streaming platform’s greatest masterpieces, which defiantly raised the bar for what animated TV and adaptations in general could achieve. Arcane is incredibly beautiful, so much so that viewers are able to pause at almost any frame and be hit with a face full of wonder. But in reality, its beauty isn’t even the show’s greatest strength; no, in fact, its most incredible achievements come from the tragedy of its characters and the consequences of their choices. Arcane is a memorable watch that lands itself on this list because, with visuals alone, it outpaces several in its genre.

2
'BoJack Horseman' (2014–2020)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/bojack-horseman-view-from-halfway-down-beatrice.jpeg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Beatrice and BoJack facing each other in 'BoJack Horseman's Season 6 episode "The View From Halfway Down"

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

BoJack Horseman masterfully mixes absurdity, sadness, emotional realism, and satire, becoming one of Netflix’s most defining animated shows. Set in a world populated by humans and anthropomorphic animals, the series focuses on BoJack Horseman (Will Arnett), a washed-up 1990s sitcom star, who is trying to reignite his fame while tackling addiction, loneliness, depression, and crippling depression.

BoJack Horseman does initially look like a pretty absurd Hollywood cartoon, but it's quite the emotional series. The show is actually extremely bleak, a mirror held up to its audience, as it doles out painfully honest examinations of depression, trauma, and the difficulty of trying to become a truly better person after repeatedly hurting those that matter. BoJack Horseman can easily claim its status as an all-time great because it’s incredibly raw and real, with a story that refuses to make light of rather serious topics and a protagonist who's extremely flawed, making it an icon in its own right.

1
'Mindhunter' (2017–2019)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/jonathan-groff-in-mindhunter.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jonathan Groff in a suit and tie walking through a prison in Mindhunter.

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

This underrated masterpiece is definitely worthy of the status as one of the all-time greatest shows ever made because it transforms crime investigation into something deeply unsettling, quiet, and intelligent. Mindhunter focuses on FBI agents Bill Tench (Holt McCallany) and Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff), who begin interviewing imprisoned serial killers in the hopes of understanding how they think and using their findings to help solve ongoing murder cases.

Mindhunter doesn’t rely on constant scenes of fast-paced arrests or acts of violence, but instead spends its runtime focusing on the difficult conversations that eventually sparked change in how serial killers were being understood. The series stands out because very few Netflix dramas are as impeccably controlled or psychologically sharp, as it delivers a fantastic procedural idea but expertly elevates it with a chilling study of obsession, behavior, power, and the language people tend to use when explaining terrible deeds. Mindhunter is one of the most deserving to be recognized as an all-time great Netflix watch because there’s never a dull moment with the captivating series, with episode after episode of brilliant precision.

items.text:
PlayStation Plus Officially Replaces October 2026 Free Game

Published Oct 2, 2026, 6:01 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

A new month is upon us, and a spooky one at that, and as always, PlayStation Plus subscribers can look forward to another batch of free titles heading to the ever-growing library. Whilst September's line-up left quite a bit to the imagination, we always live in hope that the next month will fare better, and whilst one October PS Plus addition has already been confirmed, as well as just some of the month's full offerings, the full list will be made clear over the next few weeks.

What we do know is that October's PlayStation Plus titles will include F1 25, Hunt: Showdown 1896, and Earth Defense Force: World Brothers 2. Each arriving on the service on 6 October, it is clear to see that F1 25 is the biggest pick here, whilst Hunt: Showdown 1986 offers a dark twist on the extraction shooter genre.

However, it seems as though, for some PlayStation Plus subscribers, one of these titles will not be available after being swapped out by another game entirely. According to one user over on r/PlayStationPlus, "PS Plus subscribers in Japan get Hello Neighbor instead of Hunt: Showdown 1896."

So, if you are in Japan, do not be confused if you do not gain free access to Hunt: Showdown 1896 as part of the PS Plus library this month. Instead, you will get to potentially grab Hello Neighbor, a 2017 stealth horror game which tasks players with sneaking into their neighbor's home to figure out what secret he is hiding in the basement.

It was Hello Neighbor that birthed a brand-new franchise, with it since welcoming a prequel, two multiplayer spin-offs, and a standalone sequel. Now, at time of writing, yet another sequel is currently in development, titled Hello Neighbor 3. On top of that, back in July, it was revealed that the Hello Neighbor franchise could also welcome a possible collaboration with none other than Fortnite.

It is safe to say that the Hello Neighbor series has made a name for itself over the past decade, but if you missed out on the game that started it all, and you just so happen to live in Japan, you will be able to experience Hello Neighbor at no extra cost as part of your PlayStation Plus subscription with the title being added on 6 October. However, as the Reddit user shares, "The game has also been available in the PS Plus Extra catalog for a long time (free PS5 version was added recently)."

That being said, one comment details how Hello Neighbor does not make a good replacement title, saying, "Metacritic rating of 38 on PC and 42 on Xbox, no rating for PS4/PS5. And the game has already been on Extra for a long time. It's baffling that they couldn't think of adding any other game as a replacement."

It seems as though Sony has struck again with this latest batch of titles, but if you want to ignore the reviews and check out Hello Neighbor for yourself, you can at least do so without having to spend any extra cash.
